description: Eu e meu amigo somos estudantes de Análise e Desenvolvimento de Sistemas na Fatec Rio Preto. Resolvemos participar do NASA Space Apps com o objetivo de aprimorar nossas habilidades de desenvolvimento de software e criar soluções que ajudem outras pessoas. Prezamos principalmente pelo aprendizado, cooperação, criatividade, viabilidade e funcionalidade da aplicação enquanto trabalhamos.
summary:
What did your team develop?
A web app that shows, for any landing site at the lunar south pole, where the Sun and the Earth are in the sky above the real terrain, how long until sunset and Earthset, and how two sites or two dates compare in hours of sunlight and direct line of sight to Earth.

How does it address the challenge?
Lunar Compass turns validated NASA/JPL Horizons ephemeris and LRO LOLA terrain data into an interactive sky navigator. Users can inspect 8 curated south-pole sites or any custom point, track real-time Sun and Earth visibility windows, and compare landing sites or launch delays side by side with clear metrics, countdowns, and exportable reports.

Why is it important?
At the south pole the Sun only skims the horizon, so a few kilometres or a few days change how much power and Earth contact a mission gets. Existing tools are powerful but slow for quick "what if" questions. Lunar Compass answers them in seconds for planners, educators and the public.
details:
What exactly does your solution do?

- Shows the sky from 8 curated south polar sites (6 Artemis III candidate regions and the IM-1 and IM-2 CLPS sites), or from any point typed or clicked on a globe.

- Draws the real terrain outline (LOLA) with the Sun and the Earth where they actually are, at real time or at any speed, from 14 Nov 2026 to 15 Dec 2027.

- Counts down to sunset/sunrise and Earthset/Earthrise.

- Compares two scenarios side by side (hours of sunlight, Earth in view, both together, longest darkness over 7 days, 14 days or a lunar cycle) and tests a delay of one day, one week or one lunar cycle, with the landing time fixed.

- Explains the "why" to the public (Explorer mode) and exports a report (HTML/PDF, CSV, JSON).

- Works in English and Brazilian Portuguese, in any time zone, in dark or light theme, on desktop and mobile.

How does it work?

NASA/JPL Horizons gives, hour by hour, the points on the Moon directly under the Sun and the Earth. From these the engine computes the direction and elevation of both bodies for any site. For each curated site a horizon profile was computed from LOLA terrain (720 directions, up to 450 km away, including the Moon's curvature); a body counts as visible when the centre of its disc is above that horizon, seen from 2 m above the ground. Visibility windows are computed once per site and reused, so the animation costs about 1 ms per frame. For a custom point inside the polar cap, the browser downloads a reduced 240 m LOLA model and computes the horizon in a background worker; elsewhere the point is clearly labelled "geometric only".

What are the benefits?

- Speed: a "what if we land a week later?" question takes one click instead of a session in several tools.

- Honesty: every exaggeration or approximation is labelled on screen; numbers come from NASA data and are tested.

- Reach: the same screen serves a mission planner (numbers, report export) and a classroom (Explorer notes, tour).

What impact do you hope to achieve?

Help planning teams and the public see why landing site and date selection at the lunar south pole is so delicate, and support quick re-planning when schedules slip.

How is your project creative?

Instead of relying only on top-down orbital maps, Lunar Compass puts you on the lunar surface (2 m above ground) watching the Sun and Earth move across real LOLA crater rims, paired with a two-lane visibility timeline and a one-click "delay mission" comparison. Vertical heights and disc sizes are enlarged (3x, or 2x when comparing, with 1x true scale one click away) so shallow polar angles stay readable while every exaggeration is clearly stated on screen. For custom coordinates, the app keeps the initial download light (about 0.55 MB) and loads a reduced 240 m polar-cap terrain model in a Web Worker only when needed.

What factors did your team consider?

- Scientific accuracy and honesty: validating Sun and Earth positions against NASA/JPL Horizons (better than 0.01°), accounting for lunar curvature in LOLA horizons up to 450 km, clearly stating what is not modeled (eclipses, power output, radio-link budgets), and marking custom points as reduced-terrain or geometric-only.

- Serving both planners and the public: dockable panels, UTC or any IANA time zone, fixed-landing comparisons, and exportable reports alongside Explorer "Why?" notes, dark/light themes, and English/Portuguese support.

- Responsiveness in a static web app: caching visibility windows per site and offloading custom-point horizon math to a background Web Worker.

What tools, coding languages, hardware or software did you use?

TypeScript, HTML, CSS and Canvas 2D; Vite (build), Vitest (≈280 automated tests), Node.js scripts for data preparation, Web Workers; Git. AI coding assistant (Claude, by Anthropic) used for implementation support.
